video_title: Bending Spoons is Eating Silicon Valley | CEO Luca Ferrari
gist: Bending Spoons CEO Luca Ferrari details a debt-and-cash-flow-funded, buy-and-hold-forever acquisition machine that installs acquired software businesses (Air Table, Evernote, AOL, Vimeo, Meetup, StreamYard, Tractive) onto a shared in-house operating system of 50+ proprietary tools, citing half a billion monthly active users, roughly $4M revenue per core employee (up from about $1M two-three years ago), 800,000 job applications against fewer than 300 hires in 2025, and at least $100M a year saved by not buying vendor tooling. He explains why the firm is explicitly NOT buying AI-native startups (unpredictable trajectories, irrational valuations), why it routes roughly 99% of agent tokens to self-hosted open weight models to avoid frontier-model lock-in, and voices genuine existential AI fear alongside a harsh verdict on the EU's AI act.

themes.theme: What Bending Spoons buys — and won't buy

insights.claim: Bending Spoons screens hundreds of companies a year and opens active dialogue with dozens, only underwriting deals where it believes it can materially improve product, technology, monetization and organization — value-add is a hard criterion, not a nice-to-have.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Sets the filter for which private software assets are plausible Bending Spoons targets: sellers of businesses it cannot transform will not get a competitive bid from this buyer.
insights.quote: actively we may look at hundreds of companies any in any one year and uh and then we try to establish a dialogue with uh dozens uh where we see the best match

insights.claim: Bending Spoons' single non-negotiable acquisition criterion is trajectory predictability — it must be able to plot a target's path at least five years out, because it buys to hold and operate forever rather than to sell in three to five years, and it will buy shrinking businesses as long as the rate of decline is knowable.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Explains why mature, slow-growth or even declining software assets are biddable while hypergrowth assets are not — this buyer pays a predictability premium, not a growth premium.
insights.quote: We we buy to hold and operate forever, not to sell three or five years down the line.

insights.claim: Almost all of Bending Spoons' acquisition capital has come from debt and its own free cash flow rather than equity issuance, with free cash flow being the majority of capital deployed.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A leveraged, cash-flow-funded roll-up means credit markets rather than equity markets set the ceiling on deal size; lender appetite is the constraint to watch on future bids.
insights.quote: almost all of the capital we have deployed toward acquisitions has come from that uh or our own free cash flows

insights.claim: Bending Spoons deliberately shifts toward fewer, larger acquisitions — roughly five to ten per year instead of fifty small ones — because transformation effort does not scale linearly with a target's revenue potential.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Predicts continued upward drift in deal sizes, making larger venture-backed SaaS assets increasingly plausible targets and creating a live bid for late-stage private software.
insights.quote: we prefer to acquire I don't know five or 10 businesses each year but bigger than uh 50 smaller ones

insights.claim: Ferrari sees no saturation point or obvious ceiling on how large Bending Spoons' acquisition program can get, while conceding growth must eventually slow.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Management guidance that deal cadence and scale keep compounding — relevant to anyone modelling Bending Spoons as a persistent structural bidder in software M&A.
insights.quote: How big can it get? Well, so far we we we see no end in sight. There's no obvious saturation point.

insights.claim: Bending Spoons stepped outside software with the spring acquisition of Tractive, a pet-tracking and pet-health-monitoring hardware company, citing a booming pet industry as the draw.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Signals the acquirer's competence circle now extends to connected hardware and its subscriptions, widening the universe of assets it could bid on beyond pure digital.
insights.quote: we acquired a hardware company called tractive in spring which is very interesting. Uh pet uh uh tracking and uh and and and also help monitoring for pets. Pet industry is uh is booming.

insights.claim: Bending Spoons is currently not considering acquiring any AI-native startups, because their trajectories cannot be predicted and their valuations are often irrationally high, though Ferrari expects to look again once the market matures.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Removes a widely assumed exit path for AI application companies: the most active software acquirer of this cycle is explicitly not bidding on them yet.
insights.quote: right now we're not considering acquiring any of these companies

insights.claim: Ferrari's core objection to AI startups is that a company growing 100% a year with only one or two years of history could be growing 100% or 12% three years out, and that spread changes the entire valuation.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A sharp articulation of the durability question hanging over AI revenue multiples: hypergrowth with short history is uninsurable for a permanent-capital buyer.
insights.quote: when something is growing 100% a year uh it's it's very difficult and you only have one or two years of history it's very difficult to know whether it'll be growing at 100% in three years or at 12% in three years and that changes everything

insights.claim: Ferrari predicts that while some of the most sustainably valuable companies ever will emerge from the current AI cohort, most of those companies will fail or fade away.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A barbell view from an operator with deep AI deployment experience: expect extreme dispersion rather than uniform repricing across AI application companies.
insights.quote: I'm equally confident that most of these companies will fail or at least you know basically fade away

insights.claim: Ferrari describes the AI funding environment as a gold rush in which credible-seeming founders raise at billion-dollar valuations on little more than an idea and an academic or big-company track record, risking only their reputation.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Names the asymmetric-incentive mechanism inflating early-stage AI valuations — a screening warning for LPs underwriting seed and Series A AI funds.
insights.quote: it's it's a gold rush when you see people raising uh massive massive amounts of money at billion dollar valuations with pretty much nothing other than any idea

themes.theme: Why this is not private equity

insights.claim: Bending Spoons differs structurally from private equity on three axes: it is not a fund raising from limited partners, it has never sold a material business, and it integrates acquisitions rather than keeping them separable.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Comparing the company to private equity roll-ups misprices it; permanent capital plus deep integration implies an exit-free return profile with different risk.
insights.quote: we're not a fund. We don't buy to sell companies. We've never sold a material business.

insights.claim: Deep integration onto a shared platform is structurally unavailable to private equity, because an integrated asset becomes extremely difficult or impossible to carve out and sell to a subsequent buyer.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Identifies a durable competitive wedge: the integration that creates the margin advantage is precisely what a resale-oriented sponsor cannot copy.
insights.quote: this is unavailable to private equity structurally because as a private equity you want to buy a business and then sell it. if you integrate it with all the other businesses you bought or most of them you can like it's going to be extremely difficult if not if possible at all to to to sell it to someone else.

insights.claim: Roughly 60-70% of Bending Spoons' approximately 1,000-person core team (over 2,000 including acquired teams) are software engineers, AI research engineers, product designers, product managers and growth managers — a builder workforce rather than a financial-operator one.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: The headcount mix is the evidence behind the 'technology company, not PE' claim and explains why post-acquisition codebase rewrites are feasible at scale.
insights.quote: over 2,000 including all the acquired teams most people I probably 60 70% of of this pretty large team are software engineers AI research engineers product designers product managers growth managers

insights.claim: After acquiring, Bending Spoons rebuilds large parts of the codebase, re-architects cloud infrastructure, ships features, changes UX and repeatedly reinvents monetization — what is free versus premium, prices, customer segments — and says this transformation is where most of its returns originate.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Return attribution is operational rather than financial engineering, so the model's replicability depends on engineering supply, not leverage or multiple arbitrage.
insights.quote: we uh rebuild big chunks of the codebase. Re reactite the cloud infrastructure. We launch a lot of features

insights.claim: Because Bending Spoons shareholders underwrite cash redeployed into accretive acquisitions rather than the organic growth of any one product, Ferrari says he would take 5% growth with high cash conversion over 15% growth bought with heavy cash burn.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: The incentive gap is the arbitrage: single-product owners are forced to chase growth multiples and therefore under-monetize cash that this buyer will happily capitalize.
insights.quote: if 15 is achieved by burning a lot of cash for very little profit uh many years into the future, I'd rather get five and have all that extra cash being deployed toward acquisitions that are accretive

themes.theme: Air Table deal and the 2021 valuation hangover

insights.claim: Air Table was acquired at an enterprise value of approximately $1.3 billion with substantial cash still on the balance sheet, so its investors got back roughly all the capital they put in plus more.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A disclosed clearing price for a 2021-vintage high-flyer — a usable comparable for LPs marking similar late-stage SaaS positions.
insights.quote: the enterprise value was uh approximately $1.3 billion but then they still had plenty of that cash on balance sheet

insights.claim: Ferrari says Air Table's exit valuation was very much in line with public-market comparables for software businesses of similar quality, framing the outcome as a reasonable deal rather than a distressed one.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Implies late-stage private software marks are converging on public comps — the repricing mechanism venture portfolios still carrying 2021 marks must absorb.
insights.quote: the valuation at which air table exited uh was very much in line with the sus businesses of comparable quality on the public market

insights.claim: Ferrari blames 2021's excessive private valuations on investors rather than founders, arguing a company is obliged to take capital at the best valuation available and that Air Table's team was disciplined, raised less than it could have and burned little of it.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Reframes down-round exits as investor pricing errors rather than company failures, which changes how secondaries and founder track records should be priced in this cycle.
insights.quote: if if any anybody made a mistake there was the investor certainly not the company

insights.claim: Ferrari traces venture hype cycles to a specific incentive defect: investors compensated for managing as much capital as possible, and realizing returns through exit multiples rather than through the cash a business ultimately generates.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A mechanism-level explanation of recurring venture excess, useful for anticipating where the next multiple-driven bubble forms while AUM-gathering incentives persist.
insights.quote: when investors are ultimately incentivized by managing as much capital as possible as opposed to actually delivering strong returns and when returns are primarily delivered through exits uh where all that matters is the multiple not actually the cash

insights.claim: Bending Spoons' portfolio has roughly half a billion monthly active users, which Ferrari uses to rebut the characterization of its acquisitions as a graveyard of dead brands.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Half a billion monthly actives is a distribution asset in itself — a base for monetization experiments most acquirers of legacy software cannot assemble.
insights.quote: We have half a billion monthly active users. I mean, that's a lot.

insights.claim: AOL remains the fifth most used email provider in the Western world and the primary inbox for many of its tens of millions of users, despite being a roughly 40-year-old brand with no press narrative.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Quantifies the gap between media salience and actual usage — the exact mispricing Bending Spoons harvests when buying unfashionable consumer internet assets.
insights.quote: It's the best knowledge it's the fifth most used uh email provider uh in the western world.

insights.claim: Ferrari estimates that all the heavily covered email startups of the past five to ten years do not, in aggregate, add up to even 5% of AOL's email activity and user reliance.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A direct warning that press coverage and funding rounds carry near-zero information about user traction in mature consumer categories — check usage data, not narrative.
insights.quote: in aggregate these don't probably add up to even 5% of what AOL means in terms of email sent received activity people who rely on it

insights.claim: Bending Spoons treats a business being perceived as uncool as an affirmative positive, because that perception makes the asset more accessibly priced.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A stated willingness to pay only where narrative is absent means this acquirer will systematically lose auctions for hyped assets and win in overlooked ones.
insights.quote: if we find a business that's uh slightly perceived as slightly less cool, if anything, that's a good thing for us because it means it's probably also going to be priced a little bit more accessibly

themes.theme: The proprietary operating system as moat

insights.claim: Bending Spoons has spent a decade building an internal operating system of over 50 proprietary technologies covering data storage and processing, A/B testing, payment management, recruiting, credentials management and AI model orchestration, and installs each acquired company onto it.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: The integration layer, not any individual asset, is the compounding advantage — it is what makes each successive acquisition cheaper to transform.
insights.quote: We've built over the past decade an operating system of over 50 proprietary technologies

insights.claim: Ferrari estimates that building its tooling in-house rather than buying from vendors saves Bending Spoons at least $100 million a year in costs.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A concrete number on insourcing savings at roughly 1,000 core employees, and a bearish datapoint for B2B software vendors whose most sophisticated customers can now build replacements.
insights.quote: I'd wager it's at least $100 million a year in costs

insights.claim: The tooling Bending Spoons builds would be uneconomical for any of its acquired companies to build standalone, because the R&D payback only works when amortized across a growing portfolio — making it a pure scale advantage.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Defines the minimum viable scale for copying this model: sub-scale imitators cannot fund the platform layer that generates the margin uplift.
insights.quote: it would be uneconomical unrealistic for those businesses to build them

insights.claim: Bending Spoons buys standard tools where commodity quality suffices — it uses Slack and says it needs nothing more sophisticated — but builds in-house wherever its requirements exceed what vendors optimizing for the mass enterprise market will serve.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A clean build-versus-buy rule: insource only where your requirement curve exceeds the vendor's addressable market — the exact boundary at which software vendors lose their most demanding accounts.
insights.quote: We use Slack for example. We don't need a more sophisticated version of Slack. Slack is a wonderful product.

insights.claim: Bending Spoons never assigns new zero-to-one tooling to its platform teams; the business that feels the pain builds the first version, and only once it works is it handed to platform teams to refine and expand.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A transferable internal-platform principle that explains why the toolset gets adopted rather than shelved — the usual failure mode of centralized platform organizations.
insights.quote: it's never a good idea to take a platform team and task them with building something entirely new. It's much better to have the people who need it build it.

insights.claim: Improvements any portfolio business makes to a shared tool propagate to every other business, so tooling quality improves mechanically as the portfolio and headcount expand — an internal open-source flywheel.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Implies increasing returns to further M&A: each acquisition both consumes and improves the platform, so the moat widens with deal count instead of diluting.
insights.quote: that business can improve the tool almost like a a if it were a an in-house open source community and Then those improvements are propagated to benefit all the other businesses

insights.claim: Roughly 95% of Bending Spoons' code is now written by AI, confirmed by Ferrari when the host put the figure to him.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A real-world datapoint on AI code-generation penetration at a profitable, roughly 1,000-person engineering organization — directly relevant to headcount-per-revenue assumptions across software.
insights.quote: it's written by AI. Yes.

insights.claim: Bending Spoons built an internal Slack-resident agent, one per employee, that automatically inherits that employee's exact permission set across every internal platform, so it can act on codebases and customer support tools with the same access its human owner has.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Permission inheritance is the hard part of enterprise agents; a working implementation shows the architecture third-party agent vendors have to match to be useful.
insights.quote: automatically that agent will have exactly the same level of access you do across all of our platform

insights.claim: Ferrari cites a same-day Evernote bug fix in which the general manager instructed her agent to check support data for prevalence, find the root cause in the codebase, write the fix and ping the engineering lead for review — three minutes of human instruction plus one to two hours of review replacing what he says would have taken weeks.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A specific end-to-end agentic workflow already in production — the kind of proof point that shifts expectations for engineering headcount in maintained software.
insights.quote: she she spent I don't know 3 minutes to provide these instruct instructions and then I'm sure the engineering lead had to spend uh maybe an hour or two reviewing the code but the bug got fixed

insights.claim: Bending Spoons routes roughly 99% of its agent requests and tokens to self-hosted open weight models and reserves closed-weight frontier models accessed via API for only about 1% of requests — the most complex tasks and supervision.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A 99/1 routing split at a half-billion-user operator is a bearish datapoint for frontier API revenue assumptions and bullish for open-weight inference and self-hosting infrastructure.
insights.quote: we end up using open weight models we self-host. So these are basically free.

insights.claim: Bending Spoons built its own model orchestration layer that automatically picks the cheapest adequate model per task and uses frontier models as senior reviewers of cheaper models' work, which Ferrari says keeps token costs negligible at its scale.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: The supervisor-model pattern is a concrete cost-compression mechanism; if it generalizes, enterprise AI spend per unit of useful work falls much faster than headline token prices.
insights.quote: sometimes we use them again automatically to check the work that got done by the slightly less intelligent models uh as a more senior engineer would with a more junior engineer but that's way cheaper than actually doing the work

insights.claim: Ferrari argues that handing the keys to a single AI vendor is literally orders of magnitude more expensive than building your own orchestration, and creates dangerous exposure to future price increases through lock-in.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Runs directly against the prevailing enterprise-AI go-to-market narrative — a leading indicator of sophisticated buyers pushing back on frontier-model pricing power.
insights.quote: It will make you come across as AI enabled faster and more easily, but it will be I' I'd say much less effective, but certainly way more expensive. Literally orders of magnitude more expensive.

insights.claim: For narrow use cases Bending Spoons builds its own purpose-built models: its in-house Meetup recommender system benchmarks as good as frontier models on that task while costing essentially nothing to run.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Evidence that narrow specialist models still beat general frontier models on cost at equal quality, constraining how much of the application layer frontier providers can capture.
insights.quote: to the best of our benchmarking and knowledge, it's just as good as if we were to use like some of the frontier models, which obviously comes for essentially for free

insights.claim: Bending Spoons ran more than 3,000 formally recorded quantitative experiments across its products last year, with many further initiatives beyond that count.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Quantifies the experimentation throughput underpinning monetization uplift on acquired assets — the operational metric a rival roll-up would have to match.
insights.quote: last year alone uh we ran more than 3,000 experiments across our products

insights.claim: Bending Spoons received 800,000 job applications in 2025 and hired fewer than 300 people, an acceptance rate well under one in two thousand.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Employer-brand strength is a quantified input to the model: selectively injecting high-agency talent into acquired teams is one of the stated sources of value creation.
insights.quote: We had 800,000 job applications in 2025. We hired fewer than 300 people.

insights.claim: Revenue per core-team member at Bending Spoons reached about $4 million, up from roughly $1 million just two to three years ago, and Ferrari expects it to keep rising fast on a mix of scale and technology leverage.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A roughly fourfold productivity move in two to three years is the headline metric for the AI-plus-integration thesis, and management is guiding it higher.
insights.quote: the central team, $4 million in revenue per member of that team, and this has grown tremendously. it was about a million dollars uh just uh two three years ago

insights.claim: Counting all acquired teams, Bending Spoons' revenue per employee is a little under half the $4 million core-team figure — still high, but the headline number applies only to the roughly 1,000-person core team.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: An important correction for anyone benchmarking Bending Spoons against big tech on revenue per head: the blended figure is closer to $2 million.
insights.quote: if you count everybody we have on board including acquired teams it's probably a little less than half of it's still very high but a little bit less than half that number probably

insights.claim: Unwanted churn among Bending Spoons' core-team members was about 0.6% last year, against roughly 5% that Ferrari says is considered good in technology companies.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Near-zero regretted attrition is the flywheel input for tool quality and acquisition throughput; a rise in this number would be the earliest warning the model is straining.
insights.quote: we have had essentially no unwanted unwant unwanted churn

insights.claim: Ferrari attributes Bending Spoons' retention to internal mobility — a product manager who has exhausted their enthusiasm for refining Evernote note-taking can move to a platform team or to improving AOL email UX — an option structurally unavailable at a single-product company.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: The multi-asset structure is itself the retention mechanism, so the employer-brand advantage compounds with portfolio breadth and cannot be copied by single-product rivals.
insights.quote: at vanish booms you just raise your hand and say I feel I' you know I've exhausted my creativ creativity and excitement for Evernote what else can I do

insights.claim: Ferrari says he cannot recall a single acquired business whose user retention got worse after Bending Spoons took over, contradicting the assumption that aggressive cost cuts and price increases drive churn.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: If true across the portfolio, it removes the main bear case against the model — that monetization aggression erodes the very asset being bought.
insights.quote: I can't recall a single instance where retention got worse after Benny Spoons took over.

insights.claim: Employee retention inside acquired teams has held at or above pre-acquisition levels but remains materially below the core team's, sitting nearer normal technology-industry rates.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A candid admission of a two-tier culture: integration risk concentrates in acquired teams, which is where execution problems would surface first.
insights.quote: retention rates for those team members in no case are they lower than pre-benispose

themes.theme: AI risk, AGI framing and regulation

insights.claim: Ferrari dismisses AGI as a meaningful threshold, arguing that AI doing 95% of human tasks as well or better is almost as exciting and almost as scary as doing all of them, so the moment of crossing is not a noteworthy milestone.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Deflates AGI-declaration headlines as a trading catalyst; the investable variable is the continuously rising share of tasks automated, not a declared threshold.
insights.quote: I don't know that crossing it is a particularly like the moment we cross it is a particularly uh noteworthy milestone

insights.claim: Ferrari argues AI could be more dangerous than nuclear weapons because it is surgical: an actor could use it to their own benefit while causing immense damage to everybody else without destroying themselves in the process.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A misuse-asymmetry framing implying mutually-assured-destruction deterrence logic does not transfer to AI — relevant to how fast a security-driven regulatory shock could arrive.
insights.quote: I am uh equal parts enthusiastic about AI and absolutely scared shitless.

insights.claim: Ferrari argues AI capability measurement gets harder as models improve, because intelligence is not objectively measurable like height or weight and a smarter entity finds it easier to conceal what it can do.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Implies published benchmarks systematically lag true capability, which matters for anyone timing capability-driven market moves off evaluation scores.
insights.quote: we don't know how smart AI is and the smarter it gets the less we know because in general intelligence is difficult to truly measure

insights.claim: Ferrari offers an under-discussed thesis that AI models present as inherently low-ego and self-deprecating, partly because hedged wrong answers are less embarrassing for a frontier lab, so humans will systematically underestimate rather than overestimate AI capability as danger thresholds approach.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: Inverts the common 'AI is overhyped' assumption: if capability is chronically understated, safety incidents surprise to the downside, as recent security events did.
insights.quote: these AIs don't strike me as they are likely to boast. so that our perception of their capabilities tends to exceed their capabilities

insights.claim: Ferrari says AI labs cannot afford meaningful safety slowdowns because their valuations would likely drop about 90% if the market perceived them as losing ground, making caution an existential risk to the companies themselves.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A structural argument that competitive dynamics, not intent, cap lab safety investment — meaning any binding slowdown must come from outside the labs.
insights.quote: their valuations would uh probably drop 90% if there was a perception that they're losing ground

insights.claim: Ferrari calls the EU's AI act highly harmful to the industry while solving none of the real existential problems, and says no government has yet done anything meaningful about AI safety.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A European technology CEO publicly opposing the EU's flagship AI regulation is a signal of continued regulatory friction weighing on EU-domiciled AI deployment.
insights.quote: the EU uh created the AI act which I find it to be like highly harmful to the industry and solves none of these problems

insights.claim: Ferrari predicts any country adopting protectionist AI regulation to defend jobs is destined for complete irrelevance and effectively third-world status within perhaps a few decades, because global progress will not stop.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A stark sovereign-risk framing: AI adoption policy becomes a long-horizon determinant of national competitiveness and therefore of country-level asset allocation.
insights.quote: a country that does not fully embrace using AI uh is destined to complete irrelevance and basically you know becoming third world in probably maybe even just a few decades

insights.claim: Despite deploying AI in what he estimates is the 99th percentile of aggressiveness, Ferrari says today's models still have very glaring limitations across most use cases and cannot yet be trusted with the keys to your work or life.
insights.speaker: Luca Ferrari, CEO Bending Spoons
insights.so_what: A grounded capability check from a heavy production user: the gap between perceived and actual reliability is where AI application revenue expectations are most likely to disappoint.
insights.quote: I don't think we're at a point where you could hand over the keys of your life or work to AI and you could actually trust it to to add significant value
